recorded_boundaries.text: These are the premises of the universally quantified target, not independently supplied existence results.
This is the setting of the manuscript theorem; it is not a finite-instance algorithmic runtime guarantee.
The diffusion premise belongs to the first two conjuncts of value_consequences. Its final ground-state/Parisi equality has only the minimizer premise.
This records the minimizer premise of the formal interface; it does not assert that a minimizer exists.
The extensive uncut Hamiltonian need not have an operator limit. Smallness of a generator on a core alone is not the needed exponential or domain statement.

The proof first fixes outer Lipschitz constants, then inner errors, using seed truncation, the regularized inverse sine, cutoffs and Fourier approximation. Approximation is in the rooted L² norm, not merely in marginal distribution.
This query root keeps the fixed-minimizer hypothesis in scope and exposes the complete conditional scalar-to-rooted construction. It is not a declaration that a minimizer exists.

Closed witness application: attainment supplies gamma in the manuscript class U, and the universally quantified fixed-minimizer construction uses that same gamma before any finite choices are frozen. Its annotated support edge exposes the conditional argument while discharging the supplied manuscript admissibility and minimizer premises only within this use. The binding is authored source correspondence, not mechanically checked witness equality or proof acceptance.
Disjoint mask orthogonality and the Gaussian isometry control the loss. Shared descendant branches are not assumed independent. Uniform derivative bounds refer to the original grouped coordinates.
Both norm convergence and the occupation bound are hypotheses. Strong convergence or one-point distributional convergence by itself does not permit multiplying an edge correlation by √D.
Equality of seed marginals or ordinary Gram convergence does not alone prove rooted energy convergence. The displayed L-pairing calculation is a separate ingredient.
BFMVZ Theorem 1 is a fixed-depth, fixed-angle identity. It does not transfer raw seeded, masked or controlled words, give a joint n,p,D limit, or certify the construction preceding seed removal.

Measurable seed masks are permitted through bounded subsequences with Gaussian almost-everywhere convergence. Grouped finite control coordinates are essential; no dimension-free assertion is made for all flattened color coordinates.

The receiving root seed is independent of these child fields. The first-chaos identity is an identity in the shared rooted space; a marginal Gaussian law alone does not identify E(v). This is a manuscript construction, not a Lean declaration.

First fix the finite input channels and surrounding word. Helper pinning concerns all helper descendants, not only the receiver root. Individual approximating commutator factors need not preserve that subspace. Lower first responses and scalar second responses must be retained; covariance between channels cannot be discarded.

This is finite approximation of selected local rooted operations. It is not a uniform global operator-norm Trotter estimate on an extensive Hamiltonian, and no error may be multiplied by a growing vertex count.

The finite word and all angles are held fixed before D→∞. Rotated axes and a seed gate exp(−it Zs) have the corresponding rooted formulas; this calculation alone is not a transfer theorem for seeded words.

This is an existence statement for one common finite word. Cost gates, mixers, identity padding and combining adjacent equal gate types convert it to the standard alternating QAOA convention. The tree-to-SK step is still a separate theorem.
The exponential statement has its own domain and weighted Gronwall argument. It is not inferred solely from a small Hilbert–Schmidt kernel or small generator.

This realizes both the finite scalar joint law and its shifted energy pairing. It does not assert strong finite-degree convergence for the unsmoothed sign formula. Intermediate transmitted columns need not be bounded.
The full displaced packets may have occupation of order r^(−2); only their tails have uniform weighted bounds. No uniform whole-packet occupation bound is imported from the finite-word degree limit.

Some ordinary angles are of order 1/r and can be very large, but are finite before any degree or system-size limit. The theorem gives no bound on word length, angle size or an efficient search procedure.

The same vertex seed is reused in every seed gate. Compilation proceeds outer rank to inner rank: pointwise approximants, sender partitions, finite commutators, then lower ranks; raw-seed masks are compiled last. No uniformity as helper probabilities vanish or circuit length grows is claimed.
One must prove the net o(r) cancellation. Replacing a moving insertion by an O(r)-accurate approximation and subsequently multiplying that error by 1/r is not valid.
The word is finite after the projection list is fixed. This is exact finite-list ensemble control of limiting packet data, not a uniform control statement over a continuum of unknown centers.
The order is terminal cutoff, finite scalar mesh, then finite smoothing. The statement has no joint-limit or uniform-in-terminal-time rate and still allows unbounded intermediate columns.

The displacement limit uses the o(r) error and the actual insertion change. Norm remainders are transported through unitaries; an unbounded observable is not applied to an uncontrolled norm remainder.
No maximizer of the noncompact angle supremum is required; no exact optimality at finite depth is inferred.

The construction must not choose a list from its own as-yet-unproved small-r limit. The perturbation preserves the target energy by continuity; it supplies finite nonvanishing conditions, not a uniform numerical lower bound over all words.

Uniformity concerns a fixed finite calculation, bounded parameter sets and specified weighted norms. It does not imply global operator-norm convergence, a nondegenerate covariance assumption, or uniformity in growing word length.

It does not assert QAOA circuit-energy convergence.

passages.text:
The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model asks us to choose signs that
maximise a random sum of pair interactions. The Parisi formula expresses
the limiting maximum through a nondecreasing function, the **order
parameter**. We explain why a minimising order parameter cannot be
constant on any interval below one.

The proof compares two consequences of a hypothetical gap. Minimality
fixes the values and bounds the slopes of an auxiliary curve at its
endpoints. An analytic estimate makes the derivative strictly convex
between them, leaving too little area to connect the required values.
Initial and terminal gaps need separate arguments. We then return to
the spins: a theorem about their energies gives nearly optimal sign
choices differing on any prescribed positive fraction of positions up to one half,
with arbitrarily small error in that fraction.

We follow the quantitative proof in [OpenAI (2026a)][support-manuscript];
[Hong-Bin Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][chen-support] had already proved
full support by a different method. The estimate used here makes the
final contradiction a direct comparison of areas. We assume algebra
and elementary calculus, and introduce probability and cumulative mass
through calculations. The deeper analytic facts are stated where the
proof needs them. By the end of Sections 1–6, the reader should be able
to reconstruct how minimality and those inputs exclude each kind of gap,
then translate the result into a statement about spin configurations.
Section 7 gives optional calculations and answers to the short questions
in the text; the full analytic proofs remain in the cited sources.
passages.rationale: Selects full support and the contact-to-area proof, states the prerequisite and analytic-input ceiling, and identifies optional stochastic and curvature explanations. The proof now reaches the separately sourced finite-spin consequence before the optional analytic account. No typical-pair law, algorithm or comprehension outcome is claimed.

passages.text:
## 4. The full-support theorem

**Source theorem ([OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][support-manuscript]).**
In the pure, zero-field model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma$ be an
admissible integrable minimiser of $\mathcal P$. Its Stieltjes measure
has full relative support on $[0,1)$, and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing.
For every associated diffusion and every $0\le t<1$,

$$
\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]=t,\qquad
\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1.
$$

The cumulative function determines its measure uniquely; for a fixed
Brownian motion the associated diffusion is unique by the cited
regularity results. The theorem requires a minimiser,
not merely an admissible candidate. Zero field supplies $q(0)=0$;
$\xi''=1$ enters the curvature estimate. The statement does not cover
nonzero field or general mixed-spin covariance functions.
passages.rationale: Preserves the pure zero-field minimizer hypothesis, relative support domain and quantified moment conclusions of the selected source. Separates uniqueness of the Stieltjes measure and of the diffusion for a fixed Brownian motion. No density or circuit theorem is included in the selected formal support statement.

treatments.rationale: States the same pure zero-field full-support theorem and saturated moments whose alternate ordinary proof is reconstructed here. Original source/formal correspondence remains in the source-record passage; existence and further density/circuit conclusions are separate.

passages.text:
Adding a small atom at scale $s$ raises the cumulative function at
*every* later scale. It is always allowed: the total mass is not
fixed, so no compensating removal is required. Its direction is
$\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$, equal to zero before $s$ and one
from $s$ onward. Thus

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]
=\frac12\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt=:\frac12G(s).
$$

For the candidate in Figure 1, adding $\varepsilon$ mass at $s=1/2$
creates a jump of height $\varepsilon$ there and raises the entire
remaining curve by $\varepsilon$. The coefficient changes only on
that tail, but its optimised value and feedback must be recomputed:
earlier starting states also face a changed future control problem. The
first-variation theorem accounts for this dependence. Its formula
has a tail integral because that is where the coefficient changes:
$G(s)/2$ is the marginal cost of placing mass at $s$. At a minimiser,
$G(s)\ge0$ for every $s<1$.

For the two weights in Section 2, the same accounting gives

$$
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=2G(1/4)+G(3/4).
$$

Each weight is charged for its entire remaining tail. The $q$ and $G$
in this identity belong to that candidate; no optimality has been assumed.
Reducing both weights by a fraction $\varepsilon$ multiplies the
cumulative function by $1-\varepsilon$.

Suppose temporarily that this two-weight candidate minimised
$\mathcal P$. Addition would give two nonnegative costs,
$G(1/4)\ge0$ and $G(3/4)\ge0$, while the allowed reduction would give

$$
0\le-\frac12\bigl(2G(1/4)+G(3/4)\bigr).
$$

Both costs must be zero: their positive-weighted sum is nonnegative,
and the reduction forces it to be nonpositive. This is a necessary
condition under the temporary minimiser assumption, not a claim that
the two-weight candidate attains the minimum.

For a general minimiser, the same argument replaces the finite sum by
an integral. The direction $\eta=-\gamma$
is integrable, and $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$ remains admissible for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. It scales all existing mass by the same
factor. For the continuous candidate in Figure 1, it multiplies the
two nonzero slopes and the plateau height by $1-\varepsilon$;
it works for diffuse mass as well as atoms.
The weighted-sum identity becomes

$$
0\le D\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
=-\frac12\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
$$

The exchange of integration order is valid even if the total mass is
infinite. Its absolute integral is bounded by the area from Section 2:

$$
\int_{[0,1)}\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu_\gamma(ds)
=\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
\le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$

Since $G\ge0$, its integral must be zero. If $G$ were positive at a
support point, continuity would bound it below by a positive number
on a neighbourhood carrying positive mass, contradicting that zero
integral. Hence $G=0$ on the support. This is **contact**: the
nonnegative function touches zero there. The scaling argument is the
variational argument of [Chen, Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen-support],
applied with the integrable-direction formula above.

Scaling removes only mass that exists. In Figure 1, even the supported
point $1/4$ has no atom: intervals around it carry mass, but the point
itself does not. Subtracting $\varepsilon\delta_{1/4}$ would create a
downward jump. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ the cumulative values would
remain nonnegative, but the function would no longer be nondecreasing.
Support alone does not permit atom removal. We have proved contact
on the support, not that every zero of $G$ must carry mass.

### 5.2 Contact gives endpoint conditions

We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An interior
support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

At zero, if it belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. If $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$. Integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$. This one-sided argument includes
an atom at zero.

### 5.3 Strict curvature creates an impossible integral

The support is relatively closed in $[0,1)$. Starting at a missing
point, enlarge its mass-free interval until it reaches support or a
boundary of the domain. Such a maximal interval has two
support endpoints, starts at zero outside the support, or reaches one.
We treat these three cases in order; the last includes empty support.

First suppose $(r,s)$ has both endpoints in the support, with
$0\le r<s<1$. Its constant height $c$ is necessarily positive:
for $t$ inside the gap, a small relative neighbourhood of $r$ lies in
$[0,t]$ and has positive mass, so $c=\mu_\gamma([0,t])>0$.
If $r=0$, this mass is an atom at zero. Contact imposes

$$
q(r)=r,\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(r)\le1,\quad q'(s)\le1.
$$

The first two conditions require area $s-r$ under $q'$ across the gap.
A calculus model shows how strict convexity can prevent this. On the
earlier interval $[1/3,2/3]$, put $x=3t-1$ and consider the slope
$1-x(1-x)$. Its endpoints equal one, but

$$
\int_{1/3}^{2/3}[1-(3t-1)(2-3t)]\,dt
=\frac13\int_0^1[1-x(1-x)]\,dx=\frac5{18}.
$$

The missing area is $1/3-5/18=1/18$. This is a calculus model, not a
computed SK moment curve. The next input forces the actual $q'$ below
its endpoint chord in the same way.

**Strict-curvature input ([OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][support-curvature]).**
For any admissible coefficient equal to $c>0$ on an open interval,
its moment curve satisfies, strictly inside that interval,

$$
q'''(t)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Section 7.3 explains how this sign is obtained after expectation.
The gap argument uses its strict sign; it does not use the particular
number $1/1000$.
The final inequality uses $a(t,x)>0$, proved by Gaussian smoothing
on the constant interval ([OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][support-regularity]);
convexity of $\Phi$ alone would only give $a\ge0$.
Because $q'''=(q')''$, the function $q'$ is strictly convex: between
two points its graph lies strictly below their joining chord.
The moment identity makes $q'$ continuous at the endpoints, even if
$\gamma$ jumps there; higher derivatives are needed only inside the gap.
Hence

$$
q'(t)<\frac{s-t}{s-r}q'(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}q'(s)\le1
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Integration gives $q(s)-q(r)<s-r$, contradicting contact. For the candidate in Section 2,
a minimising plateau on $(1/3,2/3)$ would require the same increment
to be both equal to and strictly less than $1/3$.
passages.rationale: Two weights produce finite contact before integrable global scaling. Supported diffuse removal and an integration-only origin argument preserve admissibility and endpoint distinctions.

Then $\gamma=0$ there, so the positive-coefficient bound supplies no strictness. Instead the zero-coefficient heat identity gives $$ q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0\qquad(00$. To control a later slope, use the same chord rule on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t0. $$ Consequently $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time $$ t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}0$, and the lower bound now gives $q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one. Thus $q(t)[§5, terminal estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap). [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Remark 7][acz] had already recorded the absence of terminal plateaus. These cases exhaust the complement of the support. Contact now gives $q(t)=t$ for every interior time, and symmetry includes zero. passages.text: ## 6. Return to the spins We can now return to the arrangement of nearly optimal spin choices. A separate theorem of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5)][acz] applies at each point in the minimiser's support. Combining it with full support: for every fixed overlap $r\in[0,1)$ and tolerances $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, with probability over the couplings tending to one exponentially fast as $n\to\infty$, there exist configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $$ |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon, \qquad H_n(\sigma)/n,\ H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta. $$ If $k$ sites differ, $k/n=(1-R)/2$. The overlap tolerance therefore gives $$ \left|\frac{k}{n}-\frac{1-r}{2}\right|<\frac\varepsilon2. $$ For example, fix an energy loss $\eta>0$ per spin and take $r=1/2$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. With probability tending to one exponentially fast, the same instance has two configurations with energies per spin at least $P_*-\eta$ and a differing-site fraction between $0.24$ and $0.26$. No numerical threshold for $n$ is asserted. At target zero, the differing-site fraction can be arbitrarily close to one half. The pair may depend on the chosen target and the couplings. This is existence for each fixed target, not a statement about typically sampled pairs or a procedure for finding them. The companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§9.3, “Near-ground configurations at a prescribed overlap”](../long/reasoning-record.md#near-ground-overlaps), gives the probability bound and the covariance adjustment.
passages.rationale: Moves the separately sourced finite-spin consequence directly after completion of the support proof. States probability over couplings and the fixed order of target/tolerances, then translates overlap error to disagreement error epsilon/2. Each pair can depend on target and couplings. No typical-pair law, construction, formal acceptance, or claim that simultaneous finite-tolerance strengthening is impossible is asserted.

passages.text: ## Sources and scope of verification This account reconstructs selected parts of OpenAI's analytic manuscript. The global scaling argument for contact follows Chen's variational proof; the terminal convexity argument in Section 5.4 is an ordinary deduction from the stated curvature, contact and boundedness inputs. It is not a claim that this alternative proof has been replayed in Lean. The Lean [implementation][support-proof], [challenge statement][support-interface] and [Comparator configuration][support-config] concern a minimiser's support and moment identities. They assume a minimiser; they do not prove the external Parisi formula or attainment. The separate scalar [implementation][value-proof] and [statement][value-interface] concern the value identity and finite Gaussian approximation. Neither selected statement covers positive density, the external near-ground overlap theorem used in Section 6, or the complete QAOA circuit theorem. The implementations use [Lean 4 (de Moura–Ullrich, 2021)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37) and [mathlib (The mathlib Community, 2020)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3372885.3373824). Comparator acceptance and research-v2 extraction remain unknown; see the *Long Reasoning Record*, [§13](../long/reasoning-record.md#verification). Kernel checking establishes a declared statement under its definitions and axioms. Its correspondence with the analytic theorem, independent proof review and reader comprehension are separate questions. The links below select the editions used. - **OpenAI (2026a).** *Full support of the zero-temperature Sherrington–Kirkpatrick order parameter*, 27 September 2026. [Pinned manuscript][support-manuscript]. §2 supplies regularity, Proposition 5.1 the strict curvature estimate, §6 the support proof, and Corollary 6.4 the additional density conclusion. - **Hong-Bin Chen (2026).** *FRSB in the SK spin glass: convergence to full-interval support at zero temperature*. [Version 1][chen-support], Theorem 1.3 for earlier full support and smooth nonnegative density; Proposition 3.2 for contact by scaling the coefficient. Strictly positive density in the further-reading note uses the separate OpenAI corollary. - **Antonio Auffinger and Wei-Kuo Chen (2017).** *Parisi formula for the ground state energy in the mixed p-spin model*, Annals of Probability 45(6B), 4617–4631. [Version 2][auffinger-chen]. The variational formula and attainment used in Section 3.2. - **Aukosh Jagannath and Ian Tobasco (2016).** *A dynamic programming approach to the Parisi functional*, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 144, 3135–3150. [Version 4][jt-control]. The control method, with finite-temperature terminal data; it is not by itself the zero-temperature regularity theorem used here. - **Wei-Kuo Chen, Madeline Handschy and Gilad Lerman (2018).** *On the energy landscape of the mixed even p-spin model*, Probability Theory and Related Fields 171, 53–95. [Version 4][chl-optimality]. Proposition 4 gives the first-variation formula used in Section 5.1; the proof of Theorem 6 gives the zero-candidate descent. - **Antonio Auffinger, Wei-Kuo Chen and Qiang Zeng (2020).** *The SK model is infinite step replica symmetry breaking at zero temperature*. [Version 2][acz], Proposition 1 and Remark 7. Near-ground overlap pairs and the earlier terminal-plateau observation. - **OpenAI (2026b).** *QAOA attains the SK ground-state energy in the thermodynamic-first limit*, 25 September 2026. [Pinned manuscript][qaoa-manuscript]. The separate circuit theorem. - **Joao Basso, Edward Farhi, Kunal Marwaha, Benjamin Villalonga and Leo Zhou (2022).** *The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm at High Depth for MaxCut on Large-Girth Regular Graphs and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model*. [Full preprint, version 3][bfmvz], §7, equation (7.2). The eventual-optimality conjecture.
